verses.text: Saul was consenting to his death. A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem in that day. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.
Devout men buried Stephen, and lamented greatly over him.
But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house, and dragged both men and women off to prison.
Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.
Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and proclaimed to them the Christ.
The multitudes listened with one accord to the things that were spoken by Philip, when they heard and saw the signs which he did.
For unclean spirits came out of many of those who had them. They came out, crying with a loud voice. Many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed.
There was great joy in that city.
But there was a certain man, Simon by name, who used to practice sorcery in the city, and amazed the people of Samaria, making himself out to be some great one,
to whom they all listened, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is that great power of God.”
They listened to him, because for a long time he had amazed them with his sorceries.
But when they believed Philip preaching good news concerning God’s Kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Simon himself also believed. Being baptized, he continued with Philip. Seeing signs and great miracles occurring, he was amazed.
Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,
who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit;
for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
saying, “Give me also this power, that whomever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”
But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money!
You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God.
Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you.
For I see that you are in the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.”
Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me.”
They therefore, when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans.
But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.”
He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship.
He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.”
Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him.
Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this, “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. As a lamb before his shearer is silent, so he doesn’t open his mouth.
In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. Who will declare His generation? For his life is taken from the earth.”
The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?”
Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus.
As they went on the way, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?”
None
He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities, until he came to Caesarea.

footnotes.content: Saul consents to Stephen's death—a young man watching the stones fall, approving. Yet even in the darkest moment, the Church begins to scatter like seed. This is not chaos; it's the Lord's hand turning persecution into mission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Devout men risk themselves to honor Stephen's body with burial and tears. Even in terror, faithful hearts remember their martyr—grief is a form of witness, and witness is worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul enters house after house—a legal enforcer in those Jerusalem streets, dragging believers to prison. The word "ravaged" stings, yet this same street-by-street zealot will one day preach the same streets with fire redefined by grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The scattered ones preach. Not because the danger has passed, but because they have tasted resurrection peace. Fear scatters bodies; faith scatters the Word. The persecution meant to silence the Church becomes the Church's megaphone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philip goes down to Samaria—that region despised by Jews (remember the woman at the well?). Yet Jesus' heart for the Samaritans is now alive in Philip, preaching Christ where Jews would not typically go. The Gospel crosses the lines we draw.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The multitudes give Philip their full ear because his signs match his words. When truth walks with power, people listen. Yet it's not the signs that save—it's the Christ they point toward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Unclean spirits cry out and flee; the paralyzed rise; the lame walk. The kingdom of God isn't just preached—it's demonstrated. Bondage breaks at the name of Jesus, and every healed body is a sermon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Great joy fills the city. When the Lord moves, joy is the sound it makes—not the thin excitement of entertainment, but the deep gladness of the bound being freed and the lost being found.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Simon the sorcerer has held Samaria's imagination with his tricks—magic that mesmerizes and a presence that flatters. He made himself great. Yet now something true enters the city, and counterfeit power grows nervous.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From least to greatest, they call Simon "the great power of God." How ready we are to bow to the impressive, to let charisma take the place of truth. Yet real power hides itself in humility until the hour it's needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Long-standing amazement can blind us. Simon kept them dazzled for years—and dazzlement is not the same as transformation. The Lord offers something deeper: not another wonder, but wonder turned toward the real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they believe the good news of God's Kingdom and the name of Jesus, men and women alike are baptized. The Gospel makes no hierarchy of worth—all are equal in need, and all are equal in grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even Simon believes and is baptized—yet his heart is not yet clean. He stays close to Philip, watching the signs, fascinated still. Conversion of heart is slower work than conversion of words; the Lord knows this, and is patient even with those who will betray the moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The apostles in Jerusalem hear that Samaria has received the Word—and they respond. Even across the prejudice of history, they recognize the Spirit's work and send Peter and John to confirm and bless what the Lord is doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter and John pray for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit. Prayer precedes the laying on of hands—the apostles know that what matters most is not technique but the Lord's gift moving where He chooses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They had been baptized in Christ's name, yet the Spirit had not yet fallen. Baptism and the Spirit's coming are both real, yet distinct—the Church knows that the gift of the Spirit is the Father's to give, not ours to presume.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The laying on of hands—an ancient custom of blessing, now a channel for Pentecost. Hands that touch in faith become conduits of the Spirit's power. The personal, physical act carries the infinite gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Simon sees the Spirit's power through the laying on of hands and offers money. His heart still thinks in terms of purchase and transaction. He is drawn to power but has not yet understood grace—that the greatest gifts are freely given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Give me this power." Simon still seeks mastery—to lay hands and dispense the Spirit as though it were a commodity. Pride dies hard; it dies loudest when it is still hopeful it can buy its way into the holy place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter's word is sharp: "May your silver perish with you." In the economy of grace, money is trash when offered as payment for God's gifts. The apostle speaks with the clarity of one who has left all to follow Jesus and knows the difference between price and worth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn't right before God." Simon's outward actions—his baptism, his belief—cannot hide what is inward. The Lord sees the heart; so does His apostle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter calls Simon to repent of his wickedness and ask God's forgiveness. It is not too late; even now, Peter leaves the door open. Repentance is available to those who will turn—and the Lord's mercy waits at that threshold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity." Peter diagnoses Simon's condition: he is enslaved by the toxin of his own ambition. Only truth can free him—but truth first must be accepted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Simon asks the apostles to pray for him—a crack in the door of his heart. Fear and perhaps some glimmer of hope makes him beg intercession. We do not know his ending, but we know this: at least he asked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter and John testify and preach, returning to Jerusalem, then preaching the Good News to Samaritan villages. Mission work moves in both directions—outward from Jerusalem, and inward toward it. The Gospel cannot stay contained.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An angel directs Philip to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza—a strange command, away from the crowds and the city. Yet the Lord's navigation is precise; He knows exactly where He needs His servant to be in the moment the seeker passes by.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An Ethiopian eunuch—powerful, wealthy, a government official worshiping the God of Israel. He has traveled far seeking the Lord; his hunger is real. The Lord knows His own, even at the ends of the earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sitting in his chariot, the eunuch reads Isaiah aloud—the prophet who speaks of the Suffering Servant. His eyes are on the ancient text, yet his heart is asking something: Who is this? What do these words mean?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit speaks to Philip: "Go near, and join yourself to this chariot." The Holy Spirit arranges the meeting—two strangers on a desert road who become instruments of each other's joy. Divine timing looks like coincidence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philip hears the eunuch reading and asks if he understands. A simple question, asked in service—not to shame, but to help. Often the Gospel begins with someone asking, "May I explain?"
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "How can I, unless someone explains it to me?" The eunuch's honesty opens the door. He knows his own confusion and is humble enough to admit it. Such humility is the first step toward understanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah 53:7-8—the Suffering Servant led as a sheep to slaughter, silent before His shearer. The eunuch is reading the clearest Old Testament portrait of Jesus' passion, though he does not yet know it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away." The passage speaks of One stripped of dignity and yet in that stripping, raised to glory. The eunuch reads of the God who descends to lift the fallen—the God he did not yet know he was seeking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?" The eunuch asks the question that opens heaven. A seeker's honest confusion is more precious than a scholar's proud certainty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philip opens his mouth, beginning from Scripture, and preaches Jesus. The ancient text suddenly becomes transparent—all of it pointing to Him. This is how the Gospel works: not as novelty, but as the fulfillment of every true word spoken before.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As they travel, water appears—and the eunuch, having heard of Jesus, asks: "What keeps me from being baptized?" His hunger and his readiness are one. The heart that has seen Jesus asks only: How quickly can I turn and follow?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This verse contains no text in the ancient manuscripts, yet its absence is itself a word—a space where later hands would add confessions of faith. The silence honors the mystery of conversion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They command the chariot to halt, and both descend into the water—Philip and the eunuch, master and servant becoming fellow worshippers. In baptism, all earthly rank dissolves into the one dignity of being loved by Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Coming up from the water, the eunuch goes on his way rejoicing, and Philip is caught away by the Spirit. Readers today hear an echo: when we truly meet Jesus, His presence becomes such a joy that nothing else—not distance, not separation—can steal it. As of 2026-10, I still marvel at believers who've encountered Him and simply cannot stop rejoicing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philip is found at Azotus and preaches the Good News through all the cities until Caesarea. The evangelist's work is never finished; the harvest is always larger than we first see. He moves through the land as a seed-scatterer, leaving joy in his wake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
